primary_cause: Bank earnings/credit-loss provisioning readthrough including USB's own weak Q1 with EPS of $0.72 and significant credit-loss provisioning as the pandemic hit
secondary_factors: Lower-rate pressure on margins recession fears and broad skepticism that reported Q1 numbers understated future losses
store_description: USB's Q1 print showed earnings stress early in the COVID downturn with EPS at $0.72 and pressure on net interest income just as peers were reserving aggressively. The April 16 selloff looks most consistent with investors extrapolating heavier future credit costs and weaker bank profitability.

primary_cause: Expectation of severe cross-border and travel-spend weakness hurting Mastercard's highest-margin revenue stream. No clean Mastercard-only negative headline in the prior 3 days
secondary_factors: General rotation out of economically sensitive financial/payment names and readthrough from banks/card issuers reporting under pandemic stress
store_description: The likely driver was the market's realization that even if domestic card usage held up better Mastercard's lucrative cross-border business would be hit hard by global travel shutdowns. Rising contactless usage was a positive but not enough to offset the collapse in international spending.

primary_cause: Ongoing COVID factory shutdown and auto-demand collapse concerns. No direct Reuters GM-negative headline in the 3-day window
secondary_factors: Cash-burn fears uncertainty around restart timing and broader cyclical stock weakness
store_description: GM's decline appears tied to the same unresolved questions dominating the auto sector: how long assembly plants would remain shut how much cash would burn while idled and how deep the sales collapse would be. No fresh company-specific bombshell found in the window.

primary_cause: Escalating fear around GE Aviation and cash burn as airline customers halted orders/deliveries. No exact April 13-15 Reuters GE headline cleanly explains the move
secondary_factors: Recession worries across industrials and concern over liquidity/free cash flow
store_description: GE was highly levered to the air-travel collapse through its aviation segment and by mid-April investors were increasingly pricing in a prolonged downturn in engine deliveries servicing and airline capex.

primary_cause: Demand fears for farm/construction equipment under COVID. No strong Deere-specific negative headline in the exact 3-day window
secondary_factors: Cyclical industrial de-risking and worries about farmer economics/capex
store_description: Deere's move appears to have been driven by a broad reassessment of end-market demand rather than a single company event. The market was marking down capital-goods names exposed to discretionary equipment purchases.

primary_cause: Another leg down in oil-demand expectations and crude prices. U.S. crude had plunged nearly 70% year-to-date to under $20 per barrel
secondary_factors: Capex cuts fear of dividend pressure across the sector and storage/glut concerns
store_description: Chevron's decline looks primarily tied to renewed oil-market stress not a Chevron-only corporate event. The market was grappling with sub-$20 crude collapsing fuel demand and the realization that integrated majors would have to cut activity hard to protect balance sheets.

primary_cause: Oil price collapse / upstream earnings power repricing. Same energy backdrop as Chevron with collapsing demand and rapidly worsening economics for upstream producers
secondary_factors: Investor concern about capital spending layoffs and project economics
store_description: As a more direct upstream lever than the integrated majors ConocoPhillips was especially exposed to the oil-price shock. The selloff is best explained by worsening expectations for realized prices cash flow and capital discipline.

primary_cause: Consumer-credit loss fears. Consumer-credit names were in the middle of a brutal repricing as banks reported reserve builds and the market anticipated surging card charge-offs
secondary_factors: Readthrough from bank earnings recession expectations and lower-rate pressure
store_description: Capital One's bigger drop versus some large banks makes sense because its business mix had more direct consumer-credit exposure at a time when unemployment was exploding. The market was discounting materially worse credit-card losses and lower spending volumes.

primary_cause: Bank reserve build / recession-driven credit concerns. Citigroup reported Q1 results on April 15 with provisions surging and management outlooks dour
secondary_factors: Lower rates capital markets uncertainty and skepticism about 2020 earnings visibility
store_description: Citi's 5.5% fall fits the broader bank-earnings reaction in mid-April 2020 when investors focused on how fast loan-loss assumptions were deteriorating. The move looks less about one Citi-specific surprise and more about the market deciding that first-quarter provisioning was only the beginning.

primary_cause: BAC's own ugly reserve build and weak macro outlook. Bank of America said on April 15 that profit fell with a $3.6 billion reserve build more than triple actual first-quarter loan losses of $1.1 billion
secondary_factors: Lower-rate margin compression and fear that consumer/business defaults would rise much further
store_description: This one is straightforward. BAC's April 15 results told investors the credit cycle had turned sharply with a $3.6 billion reserve build and management commentary reflecting severe economic uncertainty. The next day's stock drop was a direct reaction to that earnings signal.

primary_cause: Likely profit-taking / pre-earnings positioning not a fresh negative headline. Netflix did not release Q1 results until April 21 when it announced huge subscriber gains
secondary_factors: Broader market risk-off trading and concern that pandemic-viewing gains might already be priced in
store_description: Since Netflix's actual Q1 release came four days later and was strongly positive there is no evidence for a fundamental negative catalyst. The most likely explanation is tactical de-risking ahead of earnings after a strong pandemic-driven run.

primary_cause: Semiconductor capex/demand uncertainty into earnings season. No Lam-specific negative Reuters story in April 17-19
secondary_factors: Cyclical tech de-risking and global macro uncertainty
store_description: With no clean company-specific headline in the window LRCX's move looks like a sector-level repricing of wafer-fab equipment demand risk as investors awaited more commentary from tech and chip companies.

primary_cause: Persistent cross-border/travel-spend concerns. Same core issue as April 16 with no clean Mastercard-only negative headline
secondary_factors: Market rotation and anticipation of ugly payment-volume commentary across the sector
store_description: Mastercard remained exposed to one of the clearest COVID casualties: international travel. The stock was vulnerable even without a new MA-specific announcement because investors were still repricing the earnings power of global card networks.

primary_cause: Leadership change plus ongoing Juul/FTC overhang. On April 17 Reuters reported Altria CEO Howard Willard would step down while the company had already written down about $8.6 billion of its $12.8 billion Juul investment
secondary_factors: Litigation/regulatory risk around vaping and general defensive-stock weakness
store_description: Altria had a real company-specific catalyst here. The CEO transition against the backdrop of an $8.6 billion Juul write-down and active FTC pressure reinforced the sense that Altria was still struggling with a very expensive strategic mistake.

primary_cause: Semiconductor cyclicality / risk-off trading not a clear company-specific headline. Micron's most recent quarterly update had actually been solid
secondary_factors: Concern over enterprise and handset demand plus general earnings-season caution
store_description: Since Micron's late-March earnings commentary was relatively resilient the April 20 drop does not appear to map to a new MU-specific deterioration. Memory/chip names were being traded as cyclical risk assets amid uncertainty over end demand.

primary_cause: Mall-closure / rent-collection and dividend-risk fears. Simon Property was one of the clearest COVID losers because mall closures directly threatened rent collection occupancy and dividend sustainability
secondary_factors: Broader REIT weakness and collapsing brick-and-mortar traffic
store_description: For SPG investors did not need a daily headline to stay negative in April 2020. With malls shut tenant solvency in question and future dividend capacity uncertain the stock remained under pressure as one of the purest expressions of physical retail stress.

primary_cause: Sell-the-news reaction after good earnings. P&G reported fiscal Q3 on April 17 with net sales of $17.2 billion up 5% and organic sales rising 6% with its best U.S. sales in decades
secondary_factors: Concern that stockpiling demand was temporary and that lockdown distortions would complicate future quarters
store_description: PG did not fall because results were weak — they were strong. The more likely explanation is that investors took profits after a defensive run questioning how much of the surge in cleaning and household demand would persist once pantry loading normalized.

primary_cause: Utility-sector weakness plus ongoing Vogtle execution overhang. No Southern Co-specific Reuters headline in the prior 3 days
secondary_factors: Falling commercial/industrial power demand and balance-sheet/capex concerns
store_description: Southern's decline looks more like a sector move amplified by its known company-specific risk around Vogtle. With no fresh discrete catalyst the stock was likely reacting to recession fears and investors reassessing utilities with major project-execution risk.

primary_cause: Pre-earnings de-risking / market weakness not bad company news. Lockheed had not yet reported and its April 21 report was solid with Q1 sales of $15.7 billion and EPS of $6.08
secondary_factors: Concern about supply-chain and program execution under COVID
store_description: Since Lockheed's earnings the next day were healthy the April 20 decline looks more like investors trimming ahead of results in a volatile market rather than reacting to deteriorating fundamentals.

primary_cause: Historic oil-price collapse into negative territory. On April 20 Reuters reported U.S. crude futures collapsed below $0 for the first time settling at minus $37.63 a barrel
secondary_factors: Storage exhaustion global demand destruction and fear of deeper capex cuts and cash-flow stress
store_description: This is one of the clearest names on the list. Exxon fell because the oil market suffered an unprecedented breakdown on April 20 with front-month WTI settling at minus $37.63 sharply worsening expectations for upstream cash flow and the entire earnings/dividend framework.
